title: Nephrotoxicity, N S A I Ds and P P Is

segs.text: Section nineteen. Nephrotoxicity. The kidneys are susceptible for four reasons. They receive a large delivery of blood, especially blood that has passed through the liver carrying metabolites. Concentrating the urine also concentrates poisons in the tubule, and the tubular cells take compounds up into themselves. Compounds can be metabolized by the kidney cells, so toxicity in place is likely. And the kidney is sensitive to endogenous vasoconstrictors.

That last reason is unique to the kidney. Filtration depends on blood flow through the arterioles. Constricting the afferent or efferent arteriole reduces blood flow and so reduces G F R. She said, if you reduce that blood flow, you're going to reduce G F R. And because the kidney concentrates solutes in its tubules and its cells, renal cells are exposed to more of a compound than the blood level suggests.

The kinds of renal injury come from a Klaassen table. They are prerenal, vasoconstriction, crystalluria, tubular toxicity, endothelial injury, glomerulopathy, and interstitial nephritis. She requires the kinds, not the drug lists. N S A I Ds are the class she worries about most, and she named three injuries for them. Interstitial nephritis, vasoconstriction and glomerulopathy. She also told the class to add P P Is, such as omeprazole, under interstitial nephritis, even though they are not on the table. The over-the-counter label limits use to two weeks, because reflux that needs a P P I longer should be checked, and because these drugs can cause interstitial nephritis.

Injury is site specific. Not every nephrotoxin damages the whole kidney, and a quiz statement saying all nephrotoxins damage the entire kidney is false. The slide lists reasons such as differences in blood flow, transport and accumulation, and the balance of bioactivation and detoxification. Her most important reason is which enzymes are expressed in which part of the nephron. Tubular toxicity and crystalluria depend more on the chemistry of the drug.

She described her father's case. A geriatric patient, allergic to aspirin, was told to take over-the-counter omeprazole for reflux while his physical was rescheduled. Months later, routine blood work showed a high serum creatinine. The only change was the P P I. The literature described P P I induced interstitial nephritis, especially in patients with an aspirin allergy. She said, that allergic response is manifesting as interstitial nephritis in some patients, so it's not like an allergic response where you get like hives. He stopped the P P I for good. Kidney injury can be silent until a creatinine is measured.
